title: Care in the rule
hookLine: check-ups and help when needed: tie your camel and trust God, and Ben Sira's honor for the physician
tomorrow: a saint asked his own body to forgive him. what did he call it?

cards: The reminder to book a check-up has been sitting in the inbox for weeks. It's possible to pray about a worry and still never call the doctor. A man once had a version of that question, about a camel.

He'd left her outside, and before he went in, he asked the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: should I tie her up and trust in God? Or leave her loose and trust? It's a fair question, and the answer is short.

teach.b: The answer, as the collection of Tirmidhi records it: tie her, and trust. Another hadith has desert Arabs asking whether they should seek medicine.

teach.h: EVERY DISEASE HAS A REMEDY, BUT AGE.
teach.b: Yes, he said, seek treatment, servants of God; God made no disease without making a remedy for it, except one: old age. That's tawakkul, trust in God, as Islam teaches it. Trust isn't leaving the rope on the ground.
You tie the camel, take the medicine, book the appointment, and then trust God with what's beyond your hands. In this teaching, seeing a doctor isn't a lack of faith. It's part of it.
Here's a neighbor who says something close.
In the book of Sirach, the Jewish sage Ben Sira writes: honor the physician, for the Lord created him, and the Lord made medicines out of the earth, and the wise won't despise them.

teach.h: SEEK THE REMEDY; PRAY, THEN THE PHYSICIAN.
teach.b: When you're sick, he says, pray, and then give the physician his place. The same two hands: prayer and the doctor. And one honest difference.
The hadith goes straight to the remedy: there is one for every disease but old age, so seek it.
Ben Sira puts prayer and turning from wrongdoing first, then gives the physician his place, and says the doctor prays too, for the treatment to go well.
Care in your rule means both: the rope, and the trust.

how: Muslims describe seeking medicine as part of tawakkul, trust in God, and Jewish and Christian readers of Sirach honor physicians as God's gift; people on other paths pray and see a doctor too. A personal rule can name regular check-ups.

games.q: what does “care in the rule” mean?
o: caring for others first and leaving yourself for last
check-ups and help written in, plus trust in God
trusting God so fully you never need a doctor's visit

games.q: the camel and the physician: tap the pairs.
p: every disease has a remedy, but old age
trust in God that includes doing your part
honor the physician, the Lord created him

s: in Islam, seeking medicine shows a lack of trust in God
the hadith says seek treatment; tying the camel is part of tawakkul.
Ben Sira tells the sick to pray and also to give the physician his place
prayer and the doctor together, in Sirach 38.
the hadith promises a remedy for every disease without exception
it names one exception: old age.

games.q: your uncle won't see a doctor about a cough. "it's in God's hands," he says. what does the camel story say?
o: tie the camel, then trust: doing your part is part of the trust.
he's right: making an appointment would show weak faith.
trust God for small things; see doctors only for emergencies.
games.why: Asked whether to tie the camel or trust, the answer was both: tie her, and trust. Another hadith says outright: seek treatment.

practice: Think of one check-up you've been putting off: a doctor, a dentist, a counselor. Pick the day you'll call, and say it once out loud. Then sit with your hands loose for the rest of the time: the camel is tied, and the rest is trust.

wordCard.voice: Care in the rule: check-ups and help written into your rule, the camel tied and the trust kept.

orig.note: Arabic: trust in God, relying on Him after doing your part.

carryVoice: Your line: care. Tie the camel, then trust; Ben Sira says honor the physician. Day 1651, rope tied.

sources.ref: Jami at-Tirmidhi 2517 (the man asks whether to tie his camel and trust, or leave it loose and trust: 'tie it and trust')
Sunan Abu Dawud 3855 (seek treatment; God has not made a disease without a remedy, except old age)
Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:1-14 (honor the physician; the Lord created medicines out of the earth; pray, then give place to the physician; physicians also pray)
